analysis.one_liner: Matches small-dollar campaign donations six-to-one with public funds to amplify ordinary voters' giving.
analysis.headline: The bill drew 163 cosponsors, including the top two House Democrats, but was referred to three committees in January 2017 and never received a hearing, markup, or vote before that Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would rewrite how House campaigns are financed. Every voter could get a $50 campaign voucher in a three-state pilot, taxpayers would get a refundable credit for up to $50 of donations to House candidates, and candidates who show real small-dollar support (1,000 in-state donors and $50,000 in small contributions) would get public matching funds of $6 for every $1 they raise from donors giving $150 or less. In exchange, participating candidates agree to tighter contribution limits, no leadership PACs, and no joint fundraising committees. It would also require every bundler, not just registered lobbyists, to disclose the money they collect for campaigns, and require electronic filing of campaign reports.
analysis.who_benefits: Candidates who run on small donations rather than large checks, and ordinary voters whose $5 or $25 donations would be multiplied six-to-one by public matching funds. The $50 tax credit and $50 voucher are designed to let people who could never afford to give large sums participate in funding elections.

how_it_helps.text: Qualified candidates receive a payment equal to 600% of the small-dollar contributions they collect from donors giving $150 or less, funded by a new 'Freedom From Influence Fund' in the Treasury.
Every taxpayer can claim a refundable credit worth 50% of up to $50 in House campaign contributions, and a pilot program would give voters $50 'My Voice Vouchers' to allocate to federal candidates.
To qualify, a candidate must show genuine grassroots support: at least 1,000 in-state small donors and $50,000 in small-dollar contributions during a 180-day qualifying period.
Participating candidates accept stricter rules in return: individual contributions capped at $1,000, personal spending capped at $10,000, and bans on joint fundraising committees and leadership PACs.
All bundlers of contributions, not just registered lobbyists, must disclose the money they raise for campaigns, and all campaign reports must be filed electronically.
Parties may make unlimited coordinated expenditures on behalf of participating candidates, but only from accounts funded by small-dollar contributions.

analysis.who_pays: Federal taxpayers, who fund the refundable tax credits and the matching-payments program through a newly appropriated Treasury fund. Large donors, bundlers, and PACs that rely on outsized influence over House campaigns would lose relative clout, since candidates who opt in can take no more than $1,000 per individual donor.
analysis.who_pays_short: Federal taxpayers; large donors' relative influence

drawbacks.text: The program is voluntary, and it does not cap independent expenditures or super PAC spending, so unlimited outside money could still outspend participating candidates and blunt the reform's effect.
It costs public money: a refundable tax credit for every eligible taxpayer plus matching payments to candidates from a new Treasury fund that requires an appropriation.
The tax credit and voucher cover only House races and are capped at $50, leaving Senate and presidential campaign financing untouched.

Critics of public financing generally argue that taxpayers should not subsidize campaigns, including for candidates whose politics they oppose; the bill's own audit and repayment provisions are an attempt to answer that objection.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The reform would make small donations far more powerful in House races and open participation to voters who cannot write large checks, at a real but bounded public cost, and the new disclosure and audit rules would make campaign money more visible. Its main structural weakness is that it is voluntary and does not touch independent super PAC spending, so big money could still dominate through side channels. The cost is modest compared with what it changes: who pays for campaigns, and whose voice counts in them.

outcome.mechanism: Referred to three House committees the day it was introduced and never scheduled for a hearing, markup, or vote before that Congress ended.

narrative.text: Representative John Sarbanes introduced the bill on January 24, 2017, joined as original cosponsors by House Democratic leaders including Nancy Pelosi, Steny Hoyer, and James Clyburn.
It was referred the same day to the Committees on House Administration, Energy and Commerce, and Ways and Means.
It attracted 163 cosponsors (162 Democrats and 1 Republican), but the action history shows no hearing, no markup, no committee vote, and no floor action at any point in the 115th Congress.
The Congress ended on January 3, 2019, without the bill ever coming to a vote.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Large donors, bundlers, and the existing campaign fundraising system: no matching program was created, no expanded bundler disclosure took effect, and House campaign financing stayed exactly as it was.

sides.party_line_note: Support was overwhelmingly Democratic: 162 of 163 cosponsors were Democrats, with just one House Republican, and no vote ever took place that could have tested bipartisanship.

industries.note: Participating candidates could accept no more than $1,000 per individual donor and no more than $10,000 of their own money, sharply shrinking the weight of large checks, and every bundler would have to disclose what they raise. For ordinary voters, that rebalances whose money counts in House elections.

Bundler disclosure expands to all bundlers, not just registered lobbyists, and multicandidate PACs could support participating candidates only out of accounts built from small-dollar contributions. Their access-for-dollars business model narrows for any candidate who opts in.

Parties gain a new tool: unlimited coordinated spending for participating candidates, but only from accounts funded by small-dollar donations. The small-dollar requirement keeps the new power tied to grassroots giving.

The bill requires stations to sell candidate ads at the lowest unit charge without preempting them, guaranteeing candidates airtime they now often lose to higher-paying advertisers. Stations lose some scheduling flexibility and premium ad slots.

industries.industry: Professional campaign fundraisers and incumbents' fundraising advantage
industries.note: The matching program and stricter contribution rules give challengers and small-donor candidates a path to competitive budgets without courting large donors, eroding the incumbent money advantage in safe districts.
